The Built Environment and the Brain:
Review of Emerging Methods
to Investigate the Impact of Viewing
Architectural Design
Nour Tawil and Simone Kühn
Abstract The symbiotic relationship between individuals and their surrounding
built environment plays a crucial role in shaping human experiences, from the inti-
macy of indoor spaces to the vastness of the outdoors, influencing thoughts, emo-
tions, and actions. Recently, research into how architecture and design affect
psychological and neurophysiological responses has gained momentum, especially
as urbanization and mental health concerns rise. Technological advancements, like
neuroimaging and virtual reality, have ushered in a new understanding of how the
human brain engages with the built environment. However, despite this growing
interest, a comprehensive exploration of how the built environment affects neuronal
mechanisms remains relatively uncharted. This chapter seeks to address this gap by
exploring methodologies at the intersection of architecture and neuroscience.
Examining the impact of viewing interior, building, and urban design on the neuro-
physiological mechanisms underlying cognitive, affective, and behavioural
responses, this review offers insights for researchers and professionals in architec-
ture and urban planning to enhance methodologies and create environments posi-
tively impacting human well-being. The chapter concludes by addressing
methodological considerations and challenges inherent in conducting neuroscien-
tific research on architectural settings, highlighting potential directions for future
research.
Keywords Built environment · Neuroimaging · Virtual reality · Brain responses ·
Architectural design · Review
N. Tawil (*)
Max Planck Institute for Human Development, Center for Environmental Neuroscience,
Berlin, Germany

Introduction
The intricate interplay between individuals and the spaces they inhabit intertwines
humanity with the constructed world. As we navigate our daily routines, various
architectural environments continuously envelope us (Evans & McCoy, 1998).
Whether within the sanctuary of our homes, the productivity hubs of our work-
places, the rejuvenating havens of our leisure spots, or the vibrant neighbourhoods
and cities we call home, built environments leave an indelible mark on our daily
lives shaping our thoughts and emotions (Robinson & Pallasmaa, 2015) and poten-
tially affecting our mental health and well-being (Wohlwill, 1976; Evans & McCoy,
1998; Gifford, 2002; Evans, 2003; Staats et al., 2003; Elliot and Maier, 2014;
Coburn et al., 2020). Complexly woven into these spaces, human life takes form in
multifaceted ways. It is an experience that goes beyond mere aesthetics and func-
tionality (Eberhard, 2009), extending its influence deep into our brains and bodies,
as famously articulated by Sir Winston Churchill: “We shape our buildings and
afterwards they shape us” (Churchill, 1943) (➔ chapters “Aesthetics of Architecture:
Emerging Insights from the Brain” by Vartanian, and “Applications of Biometrics in
Architectural and Environmental Design” by Lavdas and Sussman).
Over the years, the exploration of how the built environment impacts psychologi-
cal and neurophysiological responses has evolved into a thriving field of inquiry
(Coburn et al., 2017; Lindal & Hartig, 2013; Stamps, 2000). This interest has broad-
ened beyond a niche, engaging researchers, architects, urban design practitioners,
policymakers, and various community stakeholders seeking to understand the
diverse dimensions of the human experience within built settings (Eberhard, 2009;
Karakas & Yildiz, 2020). This imperative gains significance amidst unprecedented
rates of urbanization and a growing global incidence of mental health disorders
(Krabbendam et al., 2021; Peen et al., 2010). Key questions emerge, prompting
exploration: What aspects of architectural design trigger affective responses, allevi-
ate stress, or induce anxiety? How do architectural elements contribute to overall
well-being, from influencing emotions and cognitive performance to promoting
mental health? Can this knowledge be harnessed to craft spaces that enrich the qual-
ity of life for everyone?
Despite the considerable time spent in and around buildings, a surprising gap
exists in linking variations in architectural features to psychological states. This gap
may be attributed to methodological and disciplinary incongruences between archi-
tecture and psychology (Edelstein & Macagno, 2012; Vartanian et al., 2013).
Historically, architectural research is based on philosophical constructs and subjec-
tive interpretations, while traditional psychological research relies on observation
and subjective measures. Neuroscience was proposed to bridge this gap, suggesting
the potential of the discipline in explaining how humans perceive and navigate built
spaces and how these spaces, in turn, affect cognition, mood, and behaviour
(Gepshtein & Snider, 2019; Sternberg & Wilson, 2006). Recent advancements in
presentation methods (e.g. virtual reality) and neuroimaging techniques have fuelled
significant developments in neuroscientific research investigating architecture,

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 171
enabling real-time measurement of brain activity and providing insights into the
neural processes underlying the responses to different designs and configurations
(Higuera-Trujillo et al., 2021; Karakas & Yildiz, 2020; Rad et al., 2023).
Virtual Reality (VR), a computer-generated simulation, immerses users in sche-
matic or realistic, three-dimensional worlds, simulating physical presence in real or
fictitious indoor or outdoor settings on a “real” scale (➔ chapter “Extended Reality
in Environmental Neuroscience Research” by Li et al.). This technology serves as a
potent tool for conducting controlled experiments, allowing for the manipulation of
specific aspects of the environment while maintaining other variables constant.
Although debates persist about VR‘s ecological validity for simulating physical
environments (Kalantari et al., 2021; Sanchez-Vives & Slater, 2005), research has
demonstrated significant neural overlaps between VR and real-world experiences
(Kalantari et al., 2021). Cost-efficiency, precise tracking of participant behaviours
(Vilar et al., 2014), and the ability to present a wide range of stimuli with high real-
ism enhance the generalizability and applicability of results. There are typically two
types of virtual environments (VEs). The Cave Automatic Virtual Environment
(CAVE) includes projector screens which create a room space consisting of three
walls and a floor. Ultimately, another type includes virtual display of an enclosed,
designed space where participants enter by wearing a head-mounted device (HMD).
While CAVE provides a room-sized immersive environment, HMD offers a porta-
ble and personal VR experience.
Neuroimaging techniques, including electroencephalography (EEG), functional
magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI), and near-infrared spectroscopy (NIRS), offer
valuable perspectives into brain processes. EEG, known for its excellent temporal
resolution (Gevins et al., 1999) and portability, records electrical activity through
scalp electrodes (➔ chapter “EEG for the Study of Environmental Neuroscience”
by Grassini). Table 1 depicts the major brainwaves detected by EEG and how they
are interpreted (Azzazy et al., 2021). Commercial-grade systems (e.g. Emotiv
EPOC) complement research-grade devices (Debener et al., 2012; Duvinage et al.,
2013). Although a peer-reviewed framework is needed for field-measured EEG with
commercial- grade devices (Mavros et al., 2016), these systems have been widely
utilized as they offer relatively easy to use brain–computer interfaces to classify raw
data into mental states (e.g. Affective Suite; short-term and long-term excitement,
frustration, engagement, and meditation). Another method, fMRI, visualizes brain

172 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
activity by detecting changes in blood flow and oxygenation levels, so-called blood-
oxygenation- level-dependent (BOLD) signal, which reflects neuronal activity
(Logothetis, 2003), offering insights into functional brain organization (➔ chapter
“Mapping the Human Brain with Computational Anatomy” by Draganski et al.).
Finally, NIRS measures changes in blood oxygenation and volume in the brain’s
cortical regions (Villringer et al., 1993), providing moderate spatial resolution and
tolerance to motion artefacts. A specialized form of NIRS used for functional brain
imaging is functional NIRS (fNIRS) (see also chapter “Environmental
Neurorehabilitation: Harnessing the power of the environment in rehabilitation fol-
lowing neurological conditions” by Norwood et al.). For the purpose of simplifica-
tion, we are using the term NIRS as an umbrella term for studies that used
either NIRS or fNIRS.
Often, neuroimaging methods are accompanied by other physiological measure-
ments like electrodermal activity (EDA) or galvanic skin response (GSR), heart rate
(HR) and heart rate variability (HRV), blood volume pulse (BVP), photoplethys-
mography (PPG), eye-movements, etc. While physiological measures provide
information about, for example, the autonomic nervous system’s (ANS) responses,
neuroimaging methods go a step further by directly revealing the neural mecha-
nisms at play. For instance, a study using sensors and VR demonstrated EEG’s supe-
riority over GSR and PPG in classifying architectural experiences (Zou & Ergan,
2021). Although EEG research mainly focused on frontal areas, the study also
emphasized the importance of frontal and occipital asymmetry as well as the effec-
tiveness of both frontal and back channels. In our review, we acknowledge the
nascent stage of the field, covering methods with limited channels. However, we
report results from physiological measures only when complementing neuroimag-
ing methods to limit the complexity of the chapter.
Fig. 1 Distribution of publications per year and architectural setting

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 173
Despite the surge of interest in this area, highlighted in the increasing number of
publications in recent years (Fig. 1), a systematic exploration of the neurophysio-
logical responses underlying the experience of architectural spaces remains a rela-
tively uncharted territory. This chapter outlines methodologies developed to
investigate how we respond to our built surroundings. These methods are at the
intersection of neuroscience, environmental psychology, and architecture, and
underscore the importance of bridging the gap between the physical and mental
realms. In our exploration, we acknowledge the multisensory nature of architecture
(Pallasmaa, 2014; Zumthor, 2006). However, we have deliberately focused on the
visual system to streamline the review. The results section has three main subsec-
tions representing research conducted on interior design, building design, and urban
design, following a recently developed framework for investigating architectural
design (Azzazy et al., 2021). Subdivisions are classified by mode of presentation
(images and videos, virtual environments, and naturalistic environments) on the first
level and neuroimaging methods (EEG, fMRI, NIRS) on the second. Studies are
grouped by themes. We conclude by discussing methodological considerations and
challenges inherent in conducting neuroimaging studies in architectural settings,
highlighting potential directions for future investigation.
Methods and Overview
The studies were identified through a comprehensive search across various sources.
A thorough exploration of English peer-reviewed papers was conducted using elec-
tronic databases from publishers such as PubMed, ScienceDirect, Nature, Springer,
Taylor & Francis, and Wiley, along with repositories like Google Scholar. The ini-
tial search terms encompassed topics related to architecture, the built environment,
indoor space, urban environment, neuroscience, neuroimaging, neuroarchitecture,
brain, and activity, as well as specific techniques like EEG, fMRI, and
NIRS. Additionally, we reviewed the bibliographic references of the retrieved
works. The saturation point was considered achieved when redundancy was
observed in most references.
The search was conducted between June and August 2023. The selection of
included articles was based on relevance and suitability. A total of 87 research
papers, spanning the years 2005–2023, were chosen for analysis. Figure 1 provides
an overview of the trends in publication years and the volume of publications
according to the different architectural settings (interior, building, and urban design).
Figures 2 and 3 illustrate the distribution of publications according to presenta-
tion mode (Fig. 2) and neuroimaging method (Fig. 3).

Results
Interior Design
Interior design is primarily concerned with the internal spaces within buildings.
Beyond the multi-sensory aspect of interior design, on the visual level, it involves
the arrangement and selection of elements within indoor spaces, including geome-
try, spatial configuration, colour schemes, materials, lighting, furniture, and vegeta-
tion, but also other aspects such as functionality and sustainability.

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 175
Images and Videos
Researchers often employ static visual stimuli like photographs, drawings, and 3D
representations to explore how the brain responds to interior design. Despite an
acknowledgement of the role of active exploration in the experience of architecture
(Nasar, 1994), the examination of dynamic stimuli, such as videos, remains limited
in comparison.
EEG
Evidence from EEG studies illustrates distinct neural processing of different repre-
sentations of architectural environments. Comparing real and computer-generated
bedroom images with different levels of details (N = 13), a subjective preference for
real and detailed over simpler images was observed (Grima Murcia et al., 2019).
Real images activated Brodman 31 brain area (also known as the retrosplenial area)
associated with episodic memory retrieval, while images without details engaged
areas near Brodman 18 region (also known as the occipital lobe) related to attention
to colour, shape, and visuospatial information processing. At later processing stages,
both real and images with details activated regions in the superior temporal gyrus
and parahippocampal gyrus, associated with reasoning, recognition memory, mem-
ory recall, retrieval, and the integration of visual elements into perceptual wholes.
Simpler images, such as sketches, activated the medial frontal rotation area, primar-
ily linked to internal mental calculation, memory encoding, and recognition. These
differences were attributed to image familiarity and the processing fluency theory
(Reber et al., 2004; Winkielman et al., 2006), underlying the significance of realistic
computer models in understanding the effects of the built environment.
Shifting focus to occupants’ cognitive function and mental health, 36 partici-
pants were presented with images and videos of two building interiors, a conven-
tional building and a sustainable building designed according to three sustainable
parameters: lighting, view, and spatial arrangement (Hu et al., 2021). In line with
the cognitive load theory (Choi et al., 2014), participants exhibited heightened
visual system engagement and adjusted their attentional focus and control process-
ing within the sustainable compared to the conventional environment, indicating
that sustainable built environments may facilitate a transition towards a more
actively engaged mental state akin to mindfulness and emphasizing a greater aware-
ness of the immediate surroundings over internal mental processes. This was evi-
dent through the increased theta/delta activities and greater involvement of visual
systems and corresponding decreases in frontal activity in the sustainable environ-
ment. Although the study identified several parameters as beneficial for cognitive
function, making inferences about individual effects remains difficult.
In the exploration of specific design parameters, research underscored the impact
of spatial layout and window size on human responses. One study focused on per-
ceived density, defined as the subjective judgment of the number of people fitting in
an area (Zur et al., 2023). Thirty-one participants viewed videos depicting equally

176 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
sized trapezoid-shaped apartments, where the wide wall location (with respect to
entrance or edge) and window size were varied. Lower perceived density was
observed when the wider wall was at the edge versus entrance. Wider windows were
perceived as less dense, especially when the larger wall was at the edge. Positive
affect ratings favoured broader windows, especially in the edge condition. The
study used two EEG measures associated with movement planning: event-related
desynchronization modulation (mu-rhythm) and theta power. Event-related desyn-
chronization refers to a decrease in specific brainwave frequency, and in the case of
mu-rhythm, this often occurs when an individual is engaged in motor planning or
execution. In this context, variations in theta power may indicate cognitive pro-
cesses related to planning and coordinating movements. Stronger mu-rhythm in the
right primary sensory cortex occurred when apartments became narrow with a wide
window or wide with a narrow window. Theta oscillations increased in the left pri-
mary sensory cortex for wide window conditions. It was concluded that density
perception relates to movement planning, suggesting that design parameters such as
an expanding space can modulate early spatial attention.
Building on Ulrich’s seminal work, which highlighted the positive effects of
natural environments on various psychological aspects (Ulrich, 1983; Ulrich et al.,
1991), research explored the impact of including natural elements on neurophysio-
logical responses. When examining a workplace setting (N = 38), exposure to natu-
ral views or indoor plants reduced anxiety levels, while their absence increased
tension and anxiety (Chang & Chen, 2005). Using one electrode placed on the
medial prefrontal cortex, and given that alpha activity is present during periods of
rest while beta activity is observed when an individual is awake and attentive, scenes
with nature views and indoor plants had the most significant impact on EEG-b val-
ues, while the presence of a window, irrespective of the view, had higher EEG-a
effects. Nature views also resulted in the lowest BVP readings. Self-reported anxi-
ety measures were in line with physiological data, further showing that window
views had stronger effects than indoor plants. Importantly, it seems that the density
of indoor vegetation can play a role in well-being, impacting perceived restorative-
ness, stress reduction, and selective visual attention (Rhee et al., 2023). Passively
viewing of images depicting indoor living environments with varying vegetation
densities (N = 41) revealed psychophysiological stress reduction as indoor vegeta-
tion increased, peaking at a density range of 13%–24% before plateauing. This was
evident through the perceived restorativeness scale scores, as well as the increased
relative alpha power spectral density (PSD) values in the analysis of all channels,
antero-frontal region, parietal region, and occipital region. However, beta relative
PSD in the analysis of all channels and the antero-frontal region showed a continu-
ous increase as the indoor vegetation density increased, indicating heightened selec-
tive visual attention.
In sum, EEG studies investigating interior design using images and videos high-
light neural distinctions in processing different architectural representations and
configurations. Real images activated Brodman 31 area linked to episodic memory,
while simpler, less detailed images engaged the Brodman 18 area associated with
visual processing (Grima Murcia et al., 2019). Both detailed and real images later

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 177
activated the superior temporal gyrus and parahippocampal gyrus, involved in
memory and visual integration, whereas simpler images activated the medial frontal
rotation area related to mental calculation and memory encoding. Sustainable com-
pared to conventional built environments showed heightened visual engagement,
increased theta/delta activities, and decreased frontal activity, suggesting a potential
transition to a more actively engaged mental state (Hu et al., 2021). Perceived den-
sity in trapezoid-shaped apartments, influenced by large wall location and window
size, seems to affect brain activations related to movement planning, with stronger
mu-rhythm observed in incongruent designs and increased theta oscillations in con-
ditions with wider windows (Zur et al., 2023). Research also underscores the posi-
tive impact of natural elements on neurophysiological responses, emphasizing that
window views and indoor plants significantly impacted beta values implicating
higher attention, while windows, regardless of the view, had higher effects on alpha
values, indicating rest (Chang & Chen, 2005). The findings highlight a more posi-
tive effect of windows views than indoor plants, and a higher effect of nature
than cityscape views. Finally, the density of indoor vegetation correlated with well-
being, revealing stress reduction at optimal density ranges of 13%–24%, as indi-
cated by subjective responses as well as increases in relative alpha relative PSD
values, while beta PSD values continuously increased with vegetation density, indi-
cating enhanced selective visual attention (Rhee et al., 2023).
fMRI
One of the first fMRI studies to examine the neural responses to interior design
stimuli (N = 18) concern an investigation into the effects of contours on aesthetic
judgements and approach-avoidance decisions (Vartanian et al., 2013). Curvilinear
spaces were more likely to be rated as beautiful compared with rectilinear ones, in
line with a long history of evidence within different types of stimulus domains (Bar
& Neta, 2007; Dazkir & Read, 2012; Leder & Carbon, 2005; Lundholm, 1921;
Silvia & Barona, 2009). Beauty ratings of curvilinear spaces correlated with
increased activity in the anterior cingulate cortex (ACC), which underlies emotional
salience monitoring (Taylor et al., 2008) and is part of the core circuit for aesthetic
processing (Brown et al., 2011). In contrast with a previous fMRI study on objects
(Bar & Neta, 2007), no amygdala activity was observed for rectilinear spaces.
Importantly, curvilinear spaces did not affect decisions to approach or avoid spaces,
only engaging the visual cortex, particularly the lingual and the calcarine gyri, and
not, as predicted, areas involved in planning motor movement.
A subsequent study used the same data to examine how ceiling height (high vs.
low) and enclosure (open vs. enclosed) influence neural responses (Vartanian et al.,
2015). Spaces with high ceilings were found more beautiful, consistent with earlier
findings (Baird et al., 1978), but ceiling height did not influence approach or avoid-
ance decisions. Open spaces were also considered more beautiful, while enclosed
spaces made participants more likely to respond with “exit” decisions. Neurologically,
beauty ratings showed activation in the left precuneus and left middle gyrus, related

178 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
to visuospatial processing (Kravitz et al., 2011), for high ceilings, but no regions
related to affect and pleasure. Open spaces activated the left middle temporal gyrus
and right superior temporal gyrus, associated with processing of abstract represen-
tations derived from visual motion information. In the enter–exit run, ceiling height
did not trigger activations, but enclosure did, specifically in both hemispheres’ ante-
rior midcingulate cortex (aMCC) which receives direct input from the amygdala,
suggesting a potential fear response according to the authors.
In a recent reanalysis of the data, the focus was on exploring correlations between
psychological dimensions (coherence, fascination, and hominess) and neural activa-
tion patterns. The aim was to investigate whether these correlations exhibited varia-
tions depending on whether participants were assessing beauty or making
approach-avoidance decisions (Coburn et al., 2020). Regardless of the task, the
level of fascination correlated with activity in the right lingual gyrus. Coherence
showed a correlation with activity in the left inferior occipital gyrus, but only when
participants were judging beauty. Hominess correlated with activity in the left
cuneus, but only when participants were making approach-avoidance decisions.
Neural activations did not correlate with global image properties such as self-
similarity and complexity scores. It was concluded that the valuation of architec-
tural processing in the visual cortices varies by dimension, as well as by task in the
case of coherence and hominess dimensions, highlighting that these neural signa-
tures reflect top-down influences on visual valuation rather than bottom-up psycho-
physical properties originating from the visual images themselves.
To sum up, fMRI studies investigating neural responses to images representing
interior design stimuli revealed that curvilinear spaces were more likely to be per-
ceived as beautiful, correlating with increased activity in the ACC, indicating a
pleasant and rewarding effect of curves (Vartanian et al., 2013). Subsequently,
examining the effects of ceiling height and enclosure showed that high ceilings were
considered more beautiful, activating the left precuneus and left middle gyrus
related to visuospatial processing, while open spaces, also found more beautiful,
activated the left middle temporal gyrus and right superior temporal gyrus, associ-
ated with abstract representations processing, and enclosed areas triggered aMCC
activation suggesting a potential fear response (Vartanian et al., 2015). A recent
reanalysis explored correlations between psychological dimensions and neural acti-
vation patterns in the visual processing areas, revealing that the level of fascination
correlated with activity in the right lingual gyrus regardless of the task, coherence
correlated with the left inferior occipital gyrus during beauty judgments and homi-
ness correlated with the left cuneus during approach-avoidance decisions (Coburn
et al., 2020).

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 179
Virtual Environments
Research has also employed virtual environments to investigate the impact of inte-
rior design on human emotions, cognition and spatial navigation, unveiling various
aspects of how design interacts with the human brain. We note that until present, the
most extensive portion of research has been conducted on virtual interiors using EEG.
EEG
Before delving into details of EEG studies that tested virtual interiors, we mention
that research has found consistency in the cognitive and neurophysiological
responses to virtual compared to real-world environments (Kalantari et al., 2021).
In the context of an educational facility, a study observed similar accuracy on cogni-
tive tests in both real and virtual classrooms (N = 25). No significant differences
were observed in eye blink rate and heart rate, while head acceleration and GSR
variance were lower in the virtual classroom. Generally, EEG frequency band-
power did not significantly differ, and analysis of event-related potentials (ERPs)
indicated strong similarity between the real and virtual classrooms, with the excep-
tion of executive functioning in a colour mismatch task.
Research into the neurophysiological responses to virtual interior environments
underscores the significant role of the sensorimotor system in the perception of
architectural spaces (Djebbara et al., 2019; Vecchiato et al., 2015a, b), supporting
the embodiment theories (Clark, 1999; Freedberg & Gallese, 2007). In one study,
EEG responses of 12 participants were recorded in a CAVE setup during the evalu-
ation of residential bedroom interior designs (Vecchiato et al., 2015a). Positive cor-
relations were observed between ratings of novelty, pleasantness, and comfort, with
a negative correlation between familiarity and novelty. EEG measures revealed that
interiors rated as pleasant, novel, and comfortable led to a desynchronization of the
mu-rhythm in the left sensorimotor areas, indicating involvement of embodied sim-
ulation mechanisms. Additionally, more pleasant and less familiar interiors increased
activations of the left frontal areas, particularly in the theta and alpha frequency
bands, along with the involvement of regions associated with spatial navigation,
indicating engagement of motivational factors regulating approach (Coan & Allen,
2003). An increase in comfort levels was associated with heightened theta frontal
midline activity, potentially linked to attention and positive emotional experi-
ence (Aftanas & Golocheikine, 2001). It was suggested that the cerebral processes
underlying the appreciation of architecture involve diverse mechanisms regulating
bodily, emotional, and cognitive responses. Another publication of the same data
aimed to test whether differences in virtual interior designs trigger distinct neural
circuits related to the mechanisms of embodiment (Vecchiato et al., 2015b). Higher
reported presence was associated with frontal-midline theta activation, indicating
the engagement of sensorimotor integration mechanisms. Similar patterns were
observed in familiar and comfortable VEs, with pleasant VEs exhibiting increased
theta power within visuomotor circuits and activating the alpha band in regions

180 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
associated with visuospatial exploration and processing of categorical spatial rela-
tions. The de-synchronization of the mu-rhythm characterized the perception of
pleasant and comfortable VEs, highlighting the involvement of left motor areas and
mechanisms related to embodiment. Generally, these findings indicate that EEG
correlates of architectural perception involve cerebral circuits associated with sen-
sorimotor integration, spatial navigation, and embodiment. A more recent investiga-
tion explored the influence of environmental features on early sensory processing in
a go/nogo task involving virtual transitions of different passability levels (Djebbara
et al., 2019). The study aimed to contribute to the debate on the relationship
between cognition, movement, and environment. There were significant differences
in subjective ratings and approach times based on door width in the Go but not
NoGo trials. Participants (N = 20) perceived narrow doors as more dominant but
less arousing and valence-inducing than mid and wide doors. Moreover,
they approached wide doors faster than mid and narrow ones. This suggests that
environmental affordances impact behaviour. EEG results demonstrated distinct
evoked potentials between impassable doors with limited affordances and passable
doors, particularly at frontocentral and occipital sites. These differences were most
notable between 50 and 200 milliseconds after the initial view of the environment,
indicating that affordances impact early cortical potentials. Motor-related brain
activity revealed that the narrow door elicited the highest amplitude for anterior
positivity and posterior negativity, likely due to the body not fitting well, creating a
prediction error during the transition. The findings suggest that early sensory brain
activity, even before actual movement, was influenced by affordances, and that
movement through transitions was preceded by a motor-related negative component
shaped by these affordances. In conclusion, the study proposes that an environ-
ment’s potential actions significantly impact perception, supporting enactivism as a
holistic approach to studying cognition (Jelić et al., 2016).
In the realm of wayfinding research, investigations into spatial navigation within
virtual environments emphasized the significant impact of architectural cues on spa-
tial orientation and navigation (Edelstein et al., 2008; Kalantari et al., 2022; Zhu
et al., 2022). Utilizing a CAVE system, brain responses to ambiguous and non-
ambiguous VEs were examined to test the effectiveness of cues to visual and spatial
relationships (Edelstein et al., 2008). Navigation from a first person perspec-
tive engaged a network of cortical areas, including occipital, parietal, occipitotem-
poral, and frontal areas. Differences in brain activity dynamics related to the
ambiguity of the starting position were observed, with stronger synchronization in
the theta band and stronger desynchronization in the lower alpha band in the parietal
and occipitotemporal cortex. This indicates the engagement of the parietal cortex in
processing visuospatial information, while both parietal and occipitotemporal
regions were involved in direction change and future path planning. Disorientation
was linked to increased alpha desynchronization, suggesting heightened attentional
demands for processing less informative visuospatial information. Moreover, stud-
ies in healthcare settings demonstrated that signage and interior design elements
could impact neurophysiological responses and orientation behaviours during way-
finding tasks (Kalantari et al., 2022). Environments enhanced with colours,

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 181
architectural elements, and distinct graphics on signs (condition C) showed improve-
ments in some orientation behaviours and greater neural activations (N = 63). While
findings did not translate into improved wayfinding times or decreased self-reported
stress, fatigue, or confusion, EEG data indicated increased neural processing in the
occipital cortex when viewing a sign and deciding on the next move in conditions C
and B (enhanced colours) compared to baseline. Moreover, there was a significant
desynchronization indicating higher cognitive engagement when looking at signs in
conditions B and C. Analysis also revealed an oscillatory pattern in theta-band
desynchronization after seeing a sign, with significant differences between condi-
tions C and B at 1s and 2.5s post-event, each lasting about 1s. Participants likely
integrated a broader array of environmental information and exhibited different
cognitive and behavioural responses due to variations in visual processing between
design conditions. The findings generally suggest that enhancing environmental
affordances in hospital design, such as architectural features and distinct sign pat-
terns, improved navigational cognition and orientation more effectively than colour
enhancement alone. Additionally, other studies have found that ceiling height can
also influence wayfinding behaviours. When immersing 343 participants into virtual
mazes with varying ceiling heights and objects, EEG measures collected through a
commercial-grade device revealed distinct brain activity patterns related to way-
finding and object mapping experiences (Erkan, 2018). The height of the space
affected directional behaviour both cognitively and behaviourally. High-ceiling
mazes were exited faster and easier, with better object-mapping and recall rates. In
low-ceiling space, individuals experiencing prolonged difficulties in finding their
way exhibited anxiety-related beta activity due to specific brain regions being over-
worked. Interestingly, age, gender and level of education were found to also
impact wayfinding behaviours.
Other approaches focused on how architectural elements and parameters inter-
acts with affective responses. Some researchers employed pairs of VEs manipulated
to represent two extreme ends of bipolar scales corresponding to positive and nega-
tive human experiences. For instance, relaxing versus stressful virtual educational
spaces, created by changing the level of luminance, natural daylight, colour of sur-
faces, openness of spaces, and presence or absence of visual cues, were found to
actually influence stress and anxiety (Ergan et al., 2019). Thirty-three participants
were asked to perform simple tasks in these VEs, revealing 40% higher EEG oscil-
lations in theta, alpha, and beta frequency bands across all 14 channels in the posi-
tive compared to the negative VE. GSR data showed a significant increase in the
number of peaks and peak amplitude in both environments compared to baseline,
particularly in the negative environment, indicating heightened stress and physio-
logical arousal. HRV decreased in both VEs compared to baseline, with a greater
decrease in the negative VE, although differences were not statistically significant.
Overall, analyses across sensors indicated a higher emotional response in the nega-
tive VE with combined results showing that the positive VE was not stress-
ful. Moreover, participants reported higher pleasantness, focus, and relaxation in the
positive VE. While the study demonstrated differential responses to the two VEs, it
assessed the combined effects of individual elements, preventing the identification

182 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
of the specific contribution of each factor to the observed effects. In fact, most of the
available research addressed architectural design parameters, manipulated sepa-
rately or in combinations, in a more controlled way. Factors that define a given
space were suggested to impact a perceiver’s brain responses. This encompasses
geometry and spatial configuration including form, scale, proportions (e.g. width,
ceiling height), windows, and interior layout, in addition to other characteristics
such as colour and lighting, and the inclusion of natural elements.
One fundamental aspects of architectural design explored in studies is the form
of interior spaces. For instance, research showed that walking through living spaces
with different forms displayed through a CAVE can trigger rapid emotional
responses in the ACC (N = 15), with curved shapes leading to stronger activations
and more positive affective ratings (Banaei et al., 2017). The observed changes in
ACC theta band activity suggested that they were not solely attributable to the emo-
tional effects of form features but also influenced by the cognitive processing of
architectural elements. However, other form parameters also significantly impact
emotional and cognitive processes, with factors like protrusion, curvature, propor-
tion, and scale having pronounced emotional effects in 112 designers and non-
designers (Shemesh et al., 2021, 2022). Among the effects observed, large spaces
were linked to higher dwell times, liking scores, larger pupillary diameters, and
fewer and shorter fixations, indicating positive emotional responses (Shemesh et al.,
2021). Physiological and emotional responses also varied with space proportion,
showing stronger reactions in extreme conditions. For instance, narrower spaces
caused a negative emotional response, as exhibited in the shorter dwell times, lower
liking score, as well as increased pupil dimensions, larger fixation rates, longer fixa-
tion durations, and a tendency for higher beta ratio (assessed via a commercial-
grade device). In terms of protrusion and curvature, zero curvature and asymmetry
increased pupil dimensions indicating interest as protrusion increased and curvature
decreased. High curvature, asymmetrical VEs were not positively perceived. Notably,
regardless of protrusion and symmetry, curvature produced high maximal GSR
measurements indicating strong aesthetic emotional responses. Medium curvature
with maximal protrusion resulted in the largest pupil dimensions, dwell time, and
liking scores. Unique impacts were observed for complete square and complete
sphere shapes on GSR, independent of scale, in addition to higher pupil dimensions
and a higher beta ratio for sharp rectangle spaces. Another publication relating to
the same data (Shemesh et al., 2022) further demonstrated a link between these
four geometrical properties and human emotions with similar conclusions.
Specifically, larger, simple, and symmetrical spaces evoked more positive responses,
while smaller symmetric spaces elicited negative emotions. Curved, large-scale
spaces were linked to more positive emotional reactions compared to large square
spaces. There was an inverse relationship between proportions and emotional
responsivity. A more protruded and asymmetric space, along with sharper non-
curved features, elicited a more positive emotional response. In another research, the
individual effects of varying scales were explored using a CAVE setup with 66
participants (Bower et al., 2022b). While scale did not influence autonomic indica-
tors or self-reported emotional states, an increased range in skin conductance

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 183
response (SCR) and HRV was noted across different conditions. Enlarged scale led
to increased EEG power within the beta bandwidth and elevated frontal midline
low-gamma and high-gamma power, in addition to increased left lateralization in
the gamma bandwidth. This suggests that such changes may be a physiological
marker of the scale impact. Surprisingly, no significant effects of scale were
observed in frontal midline power or lateralization in the theta or alpha bandwidths,
associated with positive emotional response (Ekman & Davidson, 1993). While
emotional processing may not directly involve scale, it could potentially impact
high-frequency oscillatory processes like working memory and decision-making
(Spitzer & Haegens, 2017), although this interpretation remains speculative.
Functional connectivity analysis revealed that enlarging or reducing scale enhanced
theta connectivity in the left temporoparietal and right frontal region, potentially
indicating that scale changes may have activated the visuospatial attentional net-
work while reducing scale increased high-gamma connectivity in the right frontopa-
rietal region (Bower et al., 2023).
As part of the overall composition of a given space, the role of ceiling height,
layout proportions, windows, and interior layout have also been scrutinized (Cruz-
Garza et al., 2022; Kalantari et al., 2023; Kim et al., 2021; Kong et al., 2022;
Llinares Millán et al., 2021). An investigation into a virtual postpartum care unit
found that ceiling height, aspect ratio, and window ratio impacted users’ relaxation-
arousal responses in 33 female participants (Kim et al., 2021). A decrease in the
poststimulation ratio of alpha to beta (RAB) waves was observed, indicating arousal,
with noted variations across the different architectural combinations. Specific lobes
of the brain, particularly the right frontal and left parietal lobes, exhibited significant
differences in relaxation-arousal responses, potentially linked to visuospatial and
categorical space processing. The study concluded with recommended design stan-
dards for these three parameters. Other researchers evaluated the sole effect of room
width on attention and memory (N = 90) within virtual educational settings (Llinares
Millán et al., 2021). Cognitive performance declined as room width increased. The
HRV-LFHF metric, related to the balance of sympathetic over parasympathetic
activity and attentional control, indicated greater sympathetic system activation in
the room with the narrower width. EEG measures collected via a commercial-grade
device revealed significant effects of width. The EEG-C3-Beta metric, which higher
values suggest increased thinking and focus, showed lower attention with increased
width. Similarly, for the EEG-CZ-Highbeta metric, which higher values denote
increased cognitive performance and alertness, a lower cognitive performance was
observed as width increases. The study found correlations between cognitive and
neurophysiological measures, concluding that increased width could lead to reduced
arousal thereby negatively impacting attention and memory performance. Another
educational setting was explored with 23 participants, finding that characteristics of
brain activity during cognitive tasks are influenced by room width as well as win-
dow location (Cruz-Garza et al., 2022). Although cognitive scores did not reveal
statistical differences between the different configurations, consistent differences in
EEG components emerged, more prominently for cognitive tasks that required
short-term memory encoding. Particularly, distinctive EEG features were observed

184 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
in the theta and alpha frequency bands across bilateral occipital, parietal, and frontal
brain regions. Connectivity analysis supported these findings, indicating alterations
in information transfer from centro-parietal to frontal electrodes across different
classroom conditions. Focusing on windows, the influence of window size, aperture
designs, and sky type on subjective and physiological responses was investigated
(N = 41) in virtual workplace environments (Kong et al., 2022). Irregular designs
were associated with higher interest, excitement, and complexity, while regular
designs, such as curtain walls, with calmness, satisfaction with exterior views, and
brightness. However, neither EEG nor electrocardiogram data were affected by
aperture design. Although subjective assessments of window sizes did not exhibit
significant differences, larger windows were correlated with enhanced beta varia-
tions and powers in the prefrontal right lobe areas. As for sky type, clear skies led to
more positive subjective responses compared to overcast skies, which were associ-
ated with greater mean theta rhythm levels in the left and right prefrontal lobe areas.
When investigating interior layouts in retail design, 45 participants were exposed to
three virtual grocery stores with increasing number of aisles, finding that a store
layout can influence product recall and cognitive workload (Kalantari et al., 2023).
Contrary to expectations, no significant correlation was found between the number
of aisles and perceived visual complexity, possibly due to the minimal contrast in
layout designs. Greater perceived complexity was associated with reduced per-
ceived attractiveness. There was a marginally significant correlation indicating that
simpler layouts were associated with better product recall. EEG data revealed mini-
mal differences during initial visual inspection, and significant differences during
the subsequent product memorization and recall. In particular, the layout with the
least number of aisles was associated with lower alpha power (desynchronization)
in the ACC region during both product memorization and recall, indicating increased
attention, cognitive engagement, and decision-making (Delaux et al., 2021).
Furthermore, the retrosplenial cortex (RSC) exhibited stronger activations in the
alpha band in the simpler layout, noting that alpha desynchronization in RSC is
typically observed during complex visual memory task and spatial navigation
(Delaux et al., 2021). Findings, therefore, confirmed that the lower product recall
scores in the more complex environments (with more aisles) were due to a higher
cognitive load and reduced processing fluency, highlighting that simpler store lay-
outs might be more effective in terms of consumer responses.
Apart from the above-discussed design parameters, colour, another significant
architectural feature, was found to play a crucial role in influencing emotional and
cognitive responses in VEs (Bower et al., 2022a; Llinares et al., 2021; Sadeghi
Habibabad et al., 2022). One study examined the influence of cold and warm colour
hues in virtual classrooms on cognitive attention and memory function of 160 uni-
versity students (Llinares et al., 2021). Spaces with cold-hues were associated with
better error rates in the attention task and higher memory performance. They also
increased sympathetic activity and reduced parasympathetic activity, indicating
heightened arousal. These spaces also exhibited higher brain activations, particu-
larly in beta and high-beta bands (measured with a commercial-grade device),
which are associated with attention and cognitive performance, indicating that

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 185
cold-hues contribute to achieving higher levels of attention, cognitive performance,
and working memory. The study showed significant correlations between psycho-
logical and physiological metrics. Focusing on the use of blue as ambient wall
colour within a CAVE (N = 18), changes in indicators of emotions were observed
(Bower et al., 2022a). Blue colour led to an increased range in respiration and SCR,
along with an insignificant drop in mean values of HRV. It also increased PSD
across all electrodes for theta, alpha, and beta brainwave frequencies, as well as
alpha frontal midline power and frontal hemispheric lateralization, indicating a
more positive emotional response (Davidson, 1992). However, there was no rela-
tionship between subjective and autonomic responses. Functional connectivity
analyses revealed heightened theta connectivity in the frontal region when blue was
present in the environment (Bower et al., 2023). In comparison with resting state,
blue colour increased activity in the low-gamma range, clustered in the right occipi-
tal region, suggesting that colour can affect cognitive processes and mental health.
Moving to artificial lighting, a study (N = 25) investigated brain responses to
artificial lighting in virtual office spaces using 17 conditions varying in illumination
(low to high) and correlated colour temperature (CCT) (warm to cool) using a
commercial- grade EEG device (Mostafavi et al., 2023). Results revealed an associa-
tion between illumination levels and CCT with particular EEG band features for
both lighting variables. Higher illumination levels affected activity in the frontal and
parietal brain regions, which are involved in cognitive processing and spatial per-
ception, respectively. Activity in these regions was correlated in a linear manner
across different EEG bands. For instance, greater illumination was linked to
increased α/θ and β/θ values at central and parietal electrodes, and decreased α/β
and α/γ values at the prefrontal electrodes. Notably, there was a consistent positive
linear association between higher beta power compared to theta power and higher
illumination in parietal regions, along with a reduction of theta power in frontal
regions associated with higher illumination. In terms of colour temperature, higher
CCT values (bluer light) positively correlated with increased power across all pri-
mary EEG bands in the frontal and left temporal brain region, particularly in the
theta, alpha, beta, and gamma bands. Additionally, CCT was negatively associated
with the α/γ ratio, signifying that bluer light was linked to lower α/γ ratios. Findings,
therefore, indicated common dynamics in brain responses to both higher illumina-
tion levels and higher “blue” CCT, such as reductions in the α/γ ratio in frontal brain
regions.
As found with other methods, the integration of natural elements has been shown
to have positive effects on emotional responses and the underlying brain activity
using commercial-grade EEG devices (Jung et al., 2023; Yeom et al., 2021). The
effectiveness of (small and large) green walls in relieving stress indoors was exam-
ined in 27 participants (Yeom et al., 2021). Self-reported stress measures indicated
that both small and large walls reduced anxiety levels although the large wall had a
slightly lesser effect. EDA measures showed that the small wall lowered partici-
pants’ arousal and anxiety levels, while the large wall heightened them. Analysis of
the relative alpha power revealed that the small wall had a higher relaxing effect
both visually and spatially, evidenced by increased activations in the parietal lobe

186 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
due to spatial awareness and in the occipital lobe due to visual stimuli. Moreover,
the small wall alleviated participants’ mental stress and mental fatigue (calculated
from relative band power), while the large wall exacerbated them. Findings sug-
gested that the small green wall had the most significant relaxing effect, while the
large green wall increased stress levels. Another study investigated how the incor-
poration of biophilic elements in hospital patient rooms affects emotional and brain
responses in 63 participants (Jung et al., 2023). Biophilic designs (with plant wall
and/or digital wall) led to an increase in low-frequency brainwave activity associ-
ated with relaxation, while decreasing high-frequency activity linked to heightened
arousal, indicating a tension-reducing effect. The frontal regions were found to con-
sistently play a significant role in classifying different design conditions, and alpha
power in the frontal regions was crucial for distinguishing between the rooms.
Additionally, self-reported assessments indicated that biophilic design elicited posi-
tive emotional changes, with plant walls contributing to a reduction in negative
emotions and a combination of plant walls and digital elements enhancing overall
emotional well-being in healthcare environments.
In sum, an extensive body of literature explored the impact of virtual interior
environments on the human brain. Notably, research emphasized the consistency in
cognitive and neurophysiological responses across real-world and VEs, particularly
classrooms (Kalantari et al., 2021). Following the embodied simulation theory,
studies have found that, indistinctly of the style, architectural perception is associ-
ated with diverse processes integrating emotional, motor, and cognitive mechanisms
(Vecchiato et al., 2015a). Further analyses highlighted the role of motor and cogni-
tive processes in evaluating architectural spaces for better interior design (Vecchiato
et al., 2015b). Recent evidence underscores that environmental affordances influ-
enced early sensory brain activity before actual movement, and that movements were
preceded by a motor-related negative component, also depending on the affor-
dances, indicating that perception is affected by an environment’s potential actions
(Djebbara et al., 2019). In wayfinding, brain responses to ambiguous and non-
ambiguous VEs revealed that navigation activated a network of areas associated
with spatial orientation (Edelstein et al., 2008). Stronger theta synchronization and
stronger lower alpha desynchronization were observed in the parietal and occipito-
temporal regions, suggesting a role of these regions in utilizing visuospatial infor-
mation, processing direction changes and planning of paths, while disorientation
was associated with increased alpha desynchronization indicative of heightened
attentional demands. In healthcare settings, enhanced environmental affordances,
such as distinct signage patterns and interior design features, led to improved orien-
tation behaviours and greater neural activations (Kalantari et al., 2022). Specifically,
there was an increased activity in the occipital cortex, higher cognitive engagement,
and an oscillatory pattern in theta-band desynchronization shortly after seeing a
sign. Moreover, high ceilings in virtual mazes were associated with distinct brain
activity patterns, influencing directional behaviour and object mapping experiences,
while also noting an impact of interindividual differences (Erkan, 2018). Other lines
of research manipulated VEs to represent extreme ends of bipolar scales, for exam-
ple, stressful/relaxing, finding higher EEG oscillations in theta, alpha, and beta

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 187
frequency bands in the positive compared with negative VE, indicating greater
activity associated with relaxation and pleasant experiences (Ergan et al., 2019).
However, most of the available research focused on specific parameters and ele-
ments tested separately or in combinations using factorial designs. Walking through
spaces with different forms triggered rapid emotional responses in the ACC when
perceiving curved shapes, emphasizing the role of architectural form in shaping
emotions (Banaei et al., 2017). In addition to curvature, protrusion, proportion, and
scale were found to have pronounced effects on emotional and neurophysiological
responses (Shemesh et al., 2021, 2022). For instance, there was a tendency for
higher beta ratio in narrow spaces as well as sharp rectangular spaces (Shemesh
et al., 2021). Exclusively testing scale, increased size resulted in amplified EEG
power in the beta frequency, raised frontal midline power in low-gamma and high-
gamma bandwidths, and heightened leftward lateralization in the gamma frequency,
suggesting these may be physiological markers of scale effects (Bower et al.,
2022b). Additionally, scale changes enhanced theta connectivity in the left tempo-
roparietal and right frontal regions, indicating activation of the visuospatial atten-
tional network and reduced scale increased high-gamma connectivity in the right
frontoparietal region (Bower et al., 2023). As for other design parameters, virtual
care units with varying ceiling height, aspect ratio, and window ratio influenced
RAB waves indicating arousal, with significant changes in the right frontal and left
parietal lobes linked to visuospatial and categorical space processing (Kim et al.,
2021). Manipulating solely room width revealed positive effects of narrower
rooms on attention and memory, with wider rooms leading to declines in cognitive
performance and reductions in beta and high-beta frequencies (Llinares Millán
et al., 2021). Other research showed that room width and window location influ-
enced brain activity during cognitive tasks that required short-term memory encod-
ing, with distinct EEG features in the theta and alpha frequency bands across
bilateral occipital, parietal, and frontal brain regions, and connectivity analysis indi-
cating changes in information transfer from centro-parietal to frontal electrodes
(Cruz-Garza et al., 2022). In terms of window composition, larger windows corre-
lated with enhanced beta variations and powers in the prefrontal right lobe, and
clear (compared to overcast) skies with decreased mean theta rhythm levels in both
the left and right prefrontal lobes, while aperture design did not affect brain activa-
tions (Kong et al., 2022). Concerning interior shelving layouts, simpler grocery
shops layouts with fewer aisles were associated with better product recall and lower
cognitive load (Kalantari et al., 2023). This was indicated by lower alpha power in
the ACC during product memorization and recall, reflecting increased atten-
tion, cognitive engagement and decision-making, as well as stronger activations in
the alpha band in the RSC, which suggests enhanced visual memory and spatial
navigation, indicating the effectiveness of simpler layouts in terms of consumer
responses (Kalantari et al., 2023). Moving to colours, cold compared to warm-hued
virtual classrooms were linked to better attention and memory performance, as well
as increased activations in beta and high-beta bands, indicating enhanced cognitive
performance and working memory (Llinares et al., 2021). The use of blue as ambi-
ent wall colour increased PSD across theta, alpha, and beta brainwave frequencies,

188 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
increased alpha frontal midline power, and promoted frontal hemispheric lateraliza-
tion, indicating a positive emotional response (Bower et al., 2022a). Moreover, it
heightened theta connectivity in the frontal region and increased activity in the low-
gamma range, clustered in the right occipital region, suggesting an impact on cogni-
tive processes and mental health (Bower et al., 2023). As for artificial lighting,
higher illuminance levels and higher CCT modulated specific brain activations
(Mostafavi et al., 2023). Higher illumination increased activity in the frontal and
parietal regions, while higher CCT (bluer light) increased power in the frontal and
left temporal regions, with both conditions showing common dynamics in
brain responses. Finally, the inclusion of natural elements has been shown to have
effects on emotional responses. A small green wall significantly reduced stress and
anxiety levels by increasing parietal and occipital lobe activations, while the large
green wall had lesser or even adverse effects on stress levels (Yeom et al., 2021). In
healthcare settings, plant and/or digital walls evoked heightened low-frequency
brainwave activity associated with relaxation and lowered high-frequency activity
linked to arousal, indicating a tension-reducing effect, with the frontal regions play-
ing a key role in distinguishing design conditions and alpha power in these regions
(Jung et al., 2023).
fMRI
To date, fMRI studies that used VR to investigate environmental stimuli have been
limited to the domain of spatial navigation (e.g., Iaria et al., 2003; Spiers & Maguire,
2007). Combining fMRI and VR presents a potent approach in neuroscientific
investigations of the built environment, allowing detailed exploration of brain activ-
ity during immersive experiences. This synergy enhances ecological validity, pro-
viding realistic simulations for studying human cognition and behaviour, and offers
high spatial resolution for mapping specific neural responses. This integrated
method holds promise for advancing our understanding of the intricate connections
between the brain and complex, real-world environments.
Naturalistic Environments
Studies have extended their scope to investigate the impact of interior design in real-
life scenarios, utilizing EEG and NIRS as primary methods. These studies high-
lighted that some architectural parameters and configurations have psychological
and neurophysiological effects on individuals.

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 189
EEG
In terms of interior layout, a study investigated how bed orientation affects sleep
quality (Hekmatmanesh et al., 2019). Polysomnography, a comprehensive test used
in sleep medicine including EEG measurements, was conducted on 21 participants
during two consecutive 1.5-hour naps over two days in rooms with different bed
orientations (east-west and north-south). The results showed that participants had a
longer total sleep time in the north-south orientation compared to the other orienta-
tion. Moreover, there was a noticeable increase in both rapid eye movement (REM)
latency and slow-wave sleep (SWS) latency in the north-south direction, with statis-
tical significance seen only for REM latency. Additionally, the count of arousals and
awakenings during sleep significantly increased in the east-west orientation. In
terms of EEG data, changes in delta, theta, and alpha frequencies were observed
based on bed orientation. The alpha band was the only one displaying a significant
energy ratio across the entire signal energy. In the north-south condition, increases
in the average energy of delta, theta, and alpha bands were observed. The study
concluded that sleeping in the north-south direction might be more beneficial than
east-west and that sleep EEG signals can be sensitive to Earth’s electromag-
netic field.
Initial explorations of real-life environments inspected the impact of colours on
brain activity, mood, and performance (Küller et al., 2009). Exposed to colourful
(red and patterned wall with black and white check-board floor) and grey full-
scale rooms for a 3-hour period each, 12 participants found both rooms slightly
unpleasant, closed, and original, with the colourful room higher in complexity while
the grey room higher in coherence. Participants’ self-reported emotional state
revealed decreased activation over time with no room colour differences, but they
felt more extraverted with higher emotional control in the grey room, while orienta-
tion (attention) and evaluation emotions remained unchanged. Neurophysiological
data indicated that the colourful compared to the grey room elicited lower alpha
rhythm suggesting higher arousal as well as lower heart rate suggesting cardiac
deceleration in environments eliciting cortical arousal. The heart rate reduction was
particularly notable in introverted participants, slowing by up to 10%, indicating
that this group of people is more susceptible to environmental stimulation. A com-
parison between a red and a blue room in a subsequent experiment during a 2-hour
exposure period (N = 24) found that the red room was perceived as more closed with
higher affection, while the blue room was considered more potent and slightly
higher in social status. Both rooms were rated similarly in terms of pleasantness,
complexity, unity, affection, and originality. In terms of emotional responses, par-
ticipants exhibited increased wakefulness and slight boredom, with no significant
differences between the red and blue conditions. Most participants wrote longer
stories in the red room although the difference was not statistically significant. EEG
and EKG recordings revealed that delta waves, associated with sleepiness, were
more abundant in the blue room. Moreover, alpha rhythm tended to be higher in the
blue room, especially in the second hour, over the left hemisphere, while beta and
theta frequencies showed no significant differences. Heart rate consistently remained

190 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
lower in the red room. These findings underscore the profound impact of colour on
physiological responses and emotional states in real environments, suggesting that
the colourful room was the most arousing, followed by the red room, with the blue
and grey rooms being the least arousing.
In terms of lighting, a study investigated the effects of direct and indirect lighting
on affective and neurophysiological responses of 28 participants in real-scale resi-
dential living rooms (Shin et al., 2015). The presence of direct and indirect lighting
combined led to a stronger sense of coolness and pleasantness. Theta oscillations
were more prominently observed in the right fronto-temporal and left temporo-
parietal areas (F4, F8, T4, TP7) when both types of lighting were present. Notably,
there was a significant positive correlation between participants’ perception of cool-
ness and the theta power in the right frontal region. This suggests that the combina-
tion of direct and indirect lighting enhanced feelings of pleasantness, influencing
subjective perceptions of the space. It was concluded that a combination of direct/
indirect lighting influenced participants’ subjective perception, with enhanced
pleasantness. The study suggested using theta oscillatory activity as a biological
marker for emotional status in lighting environments.
When it comes to natural elements, research aimed to identify the optimal index
of greenness for interior spaces in terms of psychophysiological responses and sub-
jective preference by exposing 103 participants to conditions with different green-
ness indexes (Choi et al., 2016). The 50% greenness index (i.e. amount of greenery
in the room) was predominantly subjectively preferred. While no significant differ-
ences in HRV values were observed, male participants exhibited increased variabil-
ity in cardiac normal-to-normal (NN) intervals and greater autonomic activity
compared to female participants. EEG data recorded on frontopolar and occipital
lobes revealed no significant differences, except that female participants had a
higher mean amplitude at the left occipital electrode compared to male participants.
The authors concluded that even a small amount of greenery may evoke a relaxing
effect in a limited space.
To summarize, in the exploration of real-life environments, EEG research found
that architectural parameters such as interior layout, colour, lighting, and natural
elements can affect neuronal mechanisms. The orientation of beds in a north-south
direction was found to improve sleep quality by increasing total sleep time, increas-
ing REM latency, and altering EEG frequency, particularly enhancing delta, theta,
and alpha band energies, suggesting sensitivity to Earth’s electromagnetic field and
potential advantages for sleep quality in such orientations compared to east-west
orientations (Hekmatmanesh et al., 2019). Comparing colourful and grey rooms,
lower alpha rhythm was found in colourful environments, indicating higher
arousal (Küller et al., 2009). Moreover, comparing blue and red rooms, delta and
alpha rhythms were more abundant in the blue room. Lighting studies revealed that
the combination of direct and indirect lighting in residential living spaces enhanced
feelings of coolness and pleasantness, with increased theta oscillations in the right
fronto-temporal and left temporo-parietal areas, and a significant positive correla-
tion between perceptions of coolness and theta power in the right frontal region, sug-
gesting that theta activity could serve as a biological marker for emotional responses

The Built Environment and the Brain: Review of Emerging Methods to Investigate… 191
to lighting environments (Shin et al., 2015). Transitioning to natural elements,
greenery in interior spaces was found to be optimal at a 50% greenness index, with
EEG data revealing no significant differences (Choi et al., 2016).
NIRS
In order to examine the effects of visual surroundings in the daily living environ-
ments on neurophysiological responses, a study exposed 15 participants to two
actual-size rooms with different interior designs (Tsunetsugu et al., 2005). There
were no significant differences in subjective responses. Parasympathetic activity
was dominant in the standard room, while sympathetic activity was dominant in the
designed room indicating a state of arousal. Diastolic blood pressure went down in
the standard room supporting a calm state. The regional cerebral blood flow (rCBF)
on the left frontal area significantly increased in both rooms suggesting interest. To
conclude, the standard room with common interiors caused a calm state, which was
interpreted to be due to familiarity, while the designed room caused an active state.
Building Design
Building design encompasses the overall planning and conceptualization of entire
structures. It includes the design of exteriors, facades, and the integration of archi-
tectural features that contribute to the building’s overall appearance and
functionality.
Images
EEG
Investigating brain responses in an unconventional virtual environment, 21 partici-
pants navigated through videos depicting three types of design representations:
abstract, semi-designed, and fully designed (Hakak et al., 2016). Fully designed
environments were perceived as easier to navigate but less creative, while semi-
designed spaces were liked the most. Creativity correlated with liking, but ease of
navigation did not correlate with creativity or liking except in abstract designs. EEG
data highlighted distinct brain activity patterns in the comparisons of fully-designed
with abstract and semi-designed with abstract environments, particularly in beta2
and beta3 bands, which are typically linked to sensorimotor functions such as move-
ment planning, preparation, and execution (Pavlidou et al., 2014), as well as move-
ment observation and imagination (Schnitzler et al., 1997). Abstract (compared to
designed) environments led to activations in the motor network, especially the pre-
central gyrus, suggesting that sensorimotor areas are involved in the aesthetic

192 N. Tawil and S. Kühn
appreciation of abstract art, and may reflect an embodied simulation of the environ-
ment (Gallese, 2005; Gallese and Sinigaglia, 2011). The study also observed pre-
frontal cortex (PFC) activation, including ACC, dorsolateral PFC (dLPFC), and
superior prefrontal gyrus. The ACC activation in fully-designed versus abstract envi-
ronments implies an increased engagement of high level cognitive functions such as
attention (Bush et al., 2000), error detection and conflict monitoring (Weissman et
al., 2005), while activation of the dLPFC in abstract environments might reflect
conflict- induced behavioural adjustment (Mansouri et al., 2007) due to the unique
challenges and rule violations in such environments. It was concluded that navigat-
ing an abstract virtual environment requires more precentral efforts, supporting the
idea that beginning the initial design stages with an abstract environment free from
phsycial rules and constraints may enhance divergeant thinking and boost creativity
during the architectural idea generation phase.
Architectural decorum, a prevalent principle in architectural theory from the
Renaissance to the onset of modernism, denotes the suitability of a building’s
design. This concept, intricately tied to ornamentation, played a crucial role in
determining how a building conveyed its position within the broader civic and social
hierarchy (Kohane & Hill, 2001). Several EEG studies have explored how decorum
and rank influence neural responses and perception (Mecklinger et al., 2014;
Oppenheim et al., 2009; Oppenheim et al., 2010). These studies involved ERPs
recorded in response to greyscale drawings of fictitious buildings that differ in their
ranking according to the Western architectural decorum, ranging from high- to low
ranking, while participants categorized images of objects and buildings. Ornaments
designating a building as high-ranking are thought to make these buildings more
prominent and therefore more memorable. If this was true, high-ranking architec-
tural designs should be more familiar, at least to Western individuals. The first study
investigated this claim in 13 participants (Oppenheim et al., 2009). Subjects accu-
rately classified objects and buildings with no significant differences in response
times. Moreover, ERP responses between 300 and 600 ms post-stimulus, recorded
over frontal lobes, could reliably distinguish between the two classes of architec-
tural stimuli without participants’ awareness of these categories. Specifically, high-
ranking buildings produced N400-potentials with significantly lower amplitudes
compared to low-ranking buildings. Findings were interpreted as evidence that
high-ranking buildings evoke a stronger sense of familiarity. After this suggestion
that high-ranking buildings may leave traces of their cultural prominence in the
perceiver’s memory facilitating visual-semantic processing (Oppenheim et al.,
2009), another investigation was conducted to probe this assumption and examine
whether the hippocampus contributes to the processing of architectural ranking
(Oppenheim et al., 2010). Testing patients suffering from medial temporal lobe epi-
lepsy (TLE) with/out hippocampal sclerosis and healthy controls (N = 44), the study
found that early negative potentials (between 200 and 400 ms) effectively distin-
guished between high- and low-ranking buildings in both groups. However, late
positive potentials (LPPs) (between 400 and 600 ms) exhibited higher amplitudes in
response to high-ranking buildings but only in healthy subjects and TLE patients
without hippocampal sclerosis. These results suggest that the distinction between

high- and low-ranking buildings involves two key processes: early visual object
selection and late post-model selection, underscoring the critical contribution of the
hippocampus to the latter phase of visual object categorization. A later cross- cultural
study explored the influence of cultural expertise on the perception of high- and
low-ranking buildings, involving 17 German and 18 Chinese participants
(Mecklinger et al., 2014). Classification performance was not affected by cultural
expertise, and response times were faster for high-ranking buildings. German par-
ticipants had a smaller N350 response to high-ranking buildings compared to low-
ranking buildings at frontal and central electrode sites, while Chinese participants
showed similar N350 responses to both building types, indicating that the initial
phase of recognizing visual objects, specifically, selecting object models was made
easier for German participants when it comes to high-ranking buildings. However,
as the object identification process advanced, incorporating information from
semantic and episodic long-term memory, there was no observable distinction
between the two cultures, as both groups exhibited an enhanced late positive com-
ponents response for high-ranking buildings, with this effect extending posteriorly
for Chinese participants. It was concluded that the ability to identify architectural
hierarchy is influenced by culturally specific expertise in Western-style architecture,
particularly during the early stages of processing. Adopting a similar approach, and
comparing coloured photographs of noted-architect-designed and ordinary archi-
tectures (N = 18), master architects’ works evoked a reduced P2 amplitude and an
increased N2 amplitude, suggesting a positive emotional response and the percep-
tion of novelty in the aesthetic evaluation of architecture (Ma et al., 2015). These
findings introduce P2 and N2 as discerning neural markers for assessing the delight
and novelty aspects expressed by architectural designs.
More recently, contour shapes, a topic well-researched in various disciplines
including studies of interior environments, have also been addressed in building
design. A study explored the psychological and physiological responses to facades
with different window shapes in nine participants (Naghibi Rad et al., 2019).
Rectangular, square, circular, and semi-circular arch shapes were perceived as
pleasant, whereas triangular and triangular arch shapes were rated as unpleasant.
Analysis of ERP components (N1, P2, and P3) revealed higher brain activity for
unpleasant window shapes compared to pleasant ones, particularly in frontal (P2
component) and posterio-occipital channels (N1 through P3 peak). The N1 compo-
nent has been associated with attention to non-spatial object characteristics such as
form and colour (Hillyard and Anllo-Vento, 1998), the peak latency of P3 compo-
nent to stimulus evaluation timing and task processing demands, varying with dif-
ferences in cognitive capability (Polich, 2007), and the P2 component to feature
detection, stimulus processing (Luck et al., 1994), selective attention (Federmeier
and Kutas, 2002), and other early sensory stages (Breznitz, 2008). Moreover, there
were larger ERP amplitudes in the right hemisphere in response to all stimuli, albeit
unpleasant stimuli generated larger ERP amplitudes. P2 amplitudes were more pro-
nounced between frontal and central lobes for unpleasant than pleasant windows.
